title: Meta Failed to Catch Hundreds of AI Child Abuse Ads. Some Included Images of Real Kids
gist: Despite Meta rolling out new AI ad-review tools after WIRED's initial report led it to delete ~50 CSAM ads, researchers at the Tech Transparency Project found 250+ more CSAM ads since August (350+ since year-end) on Meta's platforms, some using real children's images and identities, many funneling to Chinese-developer 'nudification' apps; the recurrence lands amid Meta's up-to-$16.7B child-harm settlement, a New Mexico appeal over CSAM-reporting practices, and fresh inquiries from a US senator, two state AGs, and Australia's regulator.

insights.claim: Meta's new AI ad-review system, rolled out to 'better detect and block' harmful ads after WIRED's initial CSAM report, failed to stop recurrence: researchers found 250+ additional CSAM ads since the start of August, including some identical to ads Meta had already removed.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Investors should discount claims that AI-based trust-and-safety fixes resolve liability; recurrence signals ongoing compliance risk and potential for repeated fines, settlements, or ad-revenue clawback demands.
insights.quote: That AI system, however, doesn’t appear to have been entirely effective.

insights.claim: Despite Meta's stated policy that it reviews all ads before they run, hundreds of abusive ads were live before removal, and in some cases it took Meta a full week to review live ads that researchers had already reported through its own tools.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Review-time lag directly extends paid ad exposure and monetization of illegal content, widening negligence exposure beyond a simple detection-technology failure.
insights.quote: In some instances, the TTP researchers say, it took Meta a week to review live ads they had reported for containing CSAM with Meta’s tools.

themes.theme: Scale of the CSAM/Nudify Ad Problem

insights.claim: More than 350 abusive video ads have run across Meta's platforms since the end of last year, per Tech Transparency Project researchers, with many linking to 'nudification' apps tied to Chinese developers.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A 350+ ad count over roughly nine months establishes this as a sustained, systemic pattern rather than an isolated incident, relevant to sizing ongoing trust-and-safety remediation costs.
insights.quote: researchers discovered that Meta has published more than 350 of the abusive video ads since the end of last year

insights.claim: The ads collectively reached roughly 29,000 accounts in the EU and 7,000 in the UK per Meta's own ad library, plus 250+ in the US, 120 in Australia and 80 in India, though Meta does not publish granular ad-performance data for India, meaning true reach there is likely understated.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Reach metrics that vary by disclosure regime are an audit-risk flag for regulators evaluating whether Meta's ad-library transparency tools understate real-world exposure in less-regulated markets.
insights.quote: The ads were collectively shown to more than 29,000 accounts in countries across the European Union, plus around 7,000 accounts in the United Kingdom, according to data in Meta’s ad library
insights.locator: paragraph on ad reach by country

insights.claim: Meta's own statement downplays the findings, saying many flagged ads had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and it received 'under $5,000' in total ad payments from them, a framing that contrasts with TTP's much larger count of 350+ ads.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Meta's minimized dollar/impression figures versus researchers' much larger ad count is a disputed-facts pattern investors should expect to resurface in litigation and regulatory proceedings.
insights.quote: most had fewer than 200 impressions, with the company receiving “under $5,000” in ad payments.

insights.claim: Tech Transparency Project director Katie Paul frames the pattern as Meta profiting while harm continues, implying under-investment in ad review is a business choice rather than a purely technical limitation.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A profit-motive framing from a credible researcher raises the odds this becomes an ESG/reputational overhang and a talking point in ongoing litigation over Meta's child-safety practices.
insights.quote: There’s a lot of harm that can come from this all while Meta is raking in money in the process.
insights.locator: Katie Paul quote, early in piece

insights.claim: The new findings surface while Meta is already paying up to $16.7 billion to settle lawsuits over its platforms allegedly harming children and while it is separately appealing a New Mexico court decision that would require improved CSAM-reporting processes and human review.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Fresh evidence of ongoing violations during an active $16.7B settlement and a live New Mexico appeal is a contingent-liability line item; it could weaken Meta's appeal position and invite further suits.
insights.quote: amid Meta paying up to $16.7 billion to settle lawsuits over its social networks allegedly harming children
insights.locator: paragraph on TTP findings amid settlement

insights.claim: Virginia senator Mark Warner sent Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg a letter demanding action after WIRED's initial reporting, and as of this piece's publication Meta had not yet responded.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Congressional attention combined with an unanswered letter raises the probability of legislative hearings or subpoenas if the pattern isn't resolved quickly.
insights.quote: It is disappointing that Meta continues to run ads featuring child sexual abuse material and nonconsensual intimate images after it was brought to their attention

insights.claim: State attorneys general in Michigan and Florida, plus Australia's eSafety regulator, have separately opened inquiries into Meta's ad practices following WIRED's reporting, showing a multi-jurisdiction regulatory response.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Simultaneous US-state and international regulatory attention increases the chance of parallel enforcement actions or fines across multiple jurisdictions rather than a single contained case.
insights.quote: is aware of reports concerning AI‑generated child sexual abuse material appearing in advertising on Meta. This is extremely troubling, and we are actively looking into the matter.

themes.theme: Chinese Nudify-App Supply Chain & Ad-Market Arbitrage

insights.claim: Some of the abusive ads were posted by Chinese companies acting as ad 'resellers,' even though Meta's own platforms are banned inside China, showing that banned-market entities can still buy and target Meta ad inventory abroad.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Highlights a structural loophole in advertiser verification relevant to any future ad-tech regulation requiring know-your-advertiser checks, especially for jurisdictions where the platform itself is blocked.
insights.quote: some of the ads discovered by TTP researchers were posted by Chinese companies that act as ad “resellers” in the country, where Meta’s platforms are banned.

insights.claim: The broader nonconsensual 'undress'/nudify ecosystem is described as earning millions annually and expanding fast, with over 11,000 undress ads appearing on Meta's platforms since February alone according to a separate Indicator Media report.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: An 11,000-ad count from an independent report in roughly seven months indicates this is a fast-scaling, monetizable AI-misuse vertical rather than a niche problem, worth tracking as a recurring moderation-cost driver.
insights.quote: More than 11,000 undress ads have appeared on Meta’s platforms since February this year, according to a recent Indicator Media report

insights.claim: Apple says developers behind flagged apps used a bait-and-switch tactic, initially submitting App Review-compliant apps that later added nudify features, and reports 17 of 20 flagged apps already removed with action taken on the rest.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Confirms a repeatable app-store evasion pattern that spans both Apple and Google marketplaces, relevant to assessing platform liability exposure and the durability of post-hoc app-review enforcement.
insights.quote: The developers mentioned in this report initially submitted apps that are compliant with the App Review Guidelines, only to later surface nudify capabilities, which are against our rules.

insights.claim: Google's response is less specific than Apple's, citing general proactive detection and suspension of 'hundreds' of violating apps and restricting search terms like 'nudify,' without disclosing counts tied specifically to this investigation.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A vaguer, less quantified response from Google versus Apple's specific figures is a disclosure-quality gap investors and regulators may probe when comparing the two app stores' trust-and-safety rigor.
insights.quote: We continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content

insights.claim: A former Meta trust-and-safety employee says bad actors rebuild new evasion methods within a day to five days of any new detection model, describing moderation as a persistent arms race rather than a problem that can be solved once, despite Meta having ample resources.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Suggests the current reactive moderation architecture structurally cannot outpace abuse; a due-diligence flag when evaluating whether increased trust-and-safety spend alone will fix the recurrence problem versus requiring structural changes like advertiser verification.
insights.quote: Every time the platform or investigators would build a new detection model or a new way to have some type of enforcement, they quickly—within a day, maybe five days—built a new way to avoid detection.

themes.theme: Real Children's Identities Harvested for AI-Generated CSAM

insights.claim: Unlike the initial batch of 53 ads Meta removed, the new set of 250+ ads includes ones using images of real, identifiable children, including a European royal family member whose official photo was morphed into a sexual video, escalating the harm beyond purely synthetic CSAM to identity-based exploitation.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Real-identity CSAM raises distinct legal exposure (identifiable-victim claims) beyond generic AI-content moderation failures, likely increasing per-incident litigation severity.
insights.quote: Unlike the 53 ads TTP researchers initially discovered, they were able to identify images of real children in the new ads.
insights.locator: early paragraph on new ad batch

insights.claim: Researchers identified the real-world identities of four minors used in the ads, three US-based, including two teen social-media influencers with public accounts and one stock-photo model whose image had been labeled 'pre-teen' on stock photo websites, showing that publicly available influencer and stock imagery is being harvested as raw material for AI-generated CSAM.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Flags stock-photo libraries and influencer accounts as an overlooked upstream source-material vector, widening the liability and remediation scope beyond ad review alone to image-sourcing platforms.
insights.quote: One was a stock photo model that was a real person,” Paul says of the third instance. “It was actually labeled as pre-teen on the stock photo websites.
